Genesis.author: Traditionally Moses; most scholars see several sources woven together
Genesis.date: Final form around the 6th-5th centuries BC, from older traditions
Genesis.about: Creation, the early world, and the family stories of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.

Exodus.author: Traditionally Moses; most scholars see several sources woven together
Exodus.date: Final form around the 6th-5th centuries BC, from older traditions
Exodus.about: Israel's escape from slavery in Egypt, the covenant at Mount Sinai, and the building of the tabernacle.

Leviticus.author: Traditionally Moses; often linked by scholars to Israel's priests
Leviticus.date: Final form around the 6th-5th centuries BC, from older traditions
Leviticus.about: Instructions for worship, sacrifice, the priesthood and holy living, including 'love your neighbor as yourself' (19:18).

Numbers.author: Traditionally Moses; most scholars see several sources woven together
Numbers.date: Final form around the 6th-5th centuries BC, from older traditions
Numbers.about: Israel's forty years in the wilderness between Mount Sinai and the edge of the promised land.

Deuteronomy.author: Presented as Moses' farewell speeches; many scholars link its core to King Josiah's reforms
Deuteronomy.date: Core often dated to the 7th century BC
Deuteronomy.about: Moses retells the law to a new generation before they enter the promised land, urging them to love God wholeheartedly.

Joshua.author: Unknown; part of a larger history (Joshua-Kings) compiled from older sources
Joshua.about: Israel's entry into Canaan under Joshua and the division of the land among the tribes.

Judges.author: Unknown; part of the larger history running from Joshua to Kings
Judges.about: Repeated cycles of Israel turning away from God, being oppressed, and being rescued by leaders called judges, such as Deborah, Gideon and Samson.

Ruth.author: Unknown
Ruth.date: Debated; anywhere from the monarchy to after the exile
Ruth.about: A Moabite widow's loyalty to her Israelite mother-in-law. Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of King David.

1 Samuel.author: Unknown; part of the larger history running from Joshua to Kings
1 Samuel.date: Compiled around the 7th-6th centuries BC from earlier sources
1 Samuel.about: The prophet Samuel, Saul as Israel's first king, and the rise of David.

2 Samuel.author: Unknown; part of the larger history running from Joshua to Kings
2 Samuel.date: Compiled around the 7th-6th centuries BC from earlier sources
2 Samuel.about: King David's reign, his successes and his serious failures.

1 Kings.author: Unknown; part of the larger history running from Joshua to Kings
1 Kings.date: Completed during or after the exile, around 560 BC
1 Kings.about: Solomon's wisdom and temple, the kingdom splitting into Israel and Judah, and the prophet Elijah.

2 Kings.author: Unknown; part of the larger history running from Joshua to Kings
2 Kings.date: Completed during or after the exile, around 560 BC
2 Kings.about: The kings of Israel and Judah until Assyria destroys Israel (722 BC) and Babylon destroys Jerusalem (586 BC).

1 Chronicles.author: Unknown; often called 'the Chronicler'
1 Chronicles.about: Genealogies from Adam onward and a retelling of David's reign, written for the community after the exile.

2 Chronicles.author: Unknown; often called 'the Chronicler'
2 Chronicles.about: Solomon through the exile, focusing on the temple and the kings of Judah, and ending with the decree to return home.

Ezra.author: Traditionally Ezra the scribe; possibly the same circle as Chronicles
Ezra.about: Jewish exiles return from Babylon, rebuild the temple and recommit to God's law.

Nehemiah.author: Largely Nehemiah's own first-person memoir
Nehemiah.about: Nehemiah leads the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls and a renewal of the covenant.

Esther.author: Unknown
Esther.about: A Jewish queen in Persia risks her life to save her people. It explains the festival of Purim, and God is never mentioned by name.

Job.author: Unknown
Job.date: Debated; often placed around the 6th-4th centuries BC
Job.about: A righteous man loses everything and argues with his friends, and finally with God, about why the innocent suffer.

Psalm.author: Many authors; about half are attributed to David
Psalm.date: Written over centuries; collected in final form after the exile
Psalm.about: 150 songs and prayers of praise, lament, thanks and wisdom, used in worship by Jews and Christians ever since.

Proverbs.author: Traditionally Solomon, with sections credited to other sages such as Agur and Lemuel
Proverbs.date: Collected over several centuries; finished around the time of the exile or after
Proverbs.about: Short sayings about everyday life: work, speech, money, friendship, family and self-control.

Ecclesiastes.author: 'The Teacher' (Qoheleth), traditionally Solomon
Ecclesiastes.date: Most scholars date it to the 4th-3rd centuries BC
Ecclesiastes.about: A frank reflection on meaning, work, pleasure and death, concluding that life is fleeting but still a gift to enjoy.

Song of Solomon.author: Traditionally Solomon
Song of Solomon.about: Poems celebrating love between a woman and a man, also read by Jews and Christians as a picture of God's love.

Isaiah.author: The prophet Isaiah of Jerusalem; many scholars think chapters 40-66 come from later followers
Isaiah.date: 8th century BC, with later material from the exile and after
Isaiah.about: Judgment and hope for Judah, with promises of a coming servant, a righteous king, and a restored Jerusalem.

Jeremiah.author: The prophet Jeremiah, with his scribe Baruch
Jeremiah.about: Warnings to Judah before Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, Jeremiah's own struggles, and the promise of a new covenant.

Lamentations.author: Traditionally Jeremiah; unknown
Lamentations.date: Soon after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC
Lamentations.about: Five poems of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem, holding on to hope in God's faithfulness.

Ezekiel.author: Ezekiel, a priest living in exile in Babylon
Ezekiel.about: Dramatic visions of God's glory, judgment on Jerusalem, and the future renewal of Israel, including the valley of dry bones.

Daniel.author: Set in 6th-century BC Babylon; many scholars date the final form to around 165 BC
Daniel.date: Debated: the 6th century BC traditionally, or the 2nd century BC
Daniel.about: Stories of staying faithful under foreign rule, such as the lions' den, and visions of the rise and fall of empires.

Hosea.author: The prophet Hosea
Hosea.date: 8th century BC, in the northern kingdom of Israel
Hosea.about: Hosea's painful marriage becomes a picture of God's faithful love for an unfaithful people.

Joel.author: The prophet Joel
Joel.about: A locust plague becomes a call to return to God, with a promise that God's Spirit will be poured out on all people.

Amos.author: Amos, a shepherd and fig farmer from Judah
Amos.about: A fierce call for justice for the poor and a rejection of religion without righteousness: 'let justice roll down like waters.'

Obadiah.author: The prophet Obadiah
Obadiah.about: Judgment on Edom for turning on Jerusalem in its darkest hour. It is the shortest book of the Old Testament.

Jonah.author: Unknown
Jonah.date: Set in the 8th century BC; when it was written is debated
Jonah.about: A reluctant prophet runs from God, is swallowed by a great fish, and learns that God cares even for Israel's enemies.

Micah.author: The prophet Micah
Micah.about: Judgment on corrupt leaders, hope for a ruler from Bethlehem, and the call to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly.

Nahum.author: The prophet Nahum
Nahum.date: 7th century BC, before Nineveh fell in 612 BC
Nahum.about: A poem announcing the fall of Nineveh, capital of the brutal Assyrian empire.

Habakkuk.author: The prophet Habakkuk
Habakkuk.about: A prophet questions God about injustice and violence, and learns to trust and wait.

Zephaniah.author: The prophet Zephaniah
Zephaniah.date: 7th century BC, during King Josiah's reign
Zephaniah.about: Warnings of the coming 'day of the Lord' and a promise of joy for a humble remnant.

Haggai.author: The prophet Haggai
Haggai.about: Urges the Jews who returned from exile to stop neglecting the temple and rebuild it.

Zechariah.author: The prophet Zechariah; later chapters possibly by others
Zechariah.about: Night visions encouraging the rebuilding of the temple, and hope for a coming humble king.

Malachi.author: Unknown; 'Malachi' means 'my messenger'
Malachi.about: Calls the community after the exile back to faithful worship, honest marriages and care for the poor.

Matthew.author: Traditionally the apostle Matthew; the book itself is anonymous
Matthew.date: Many scholars say around AD 80-90; tradition places it earlier
Matthew.about: Jesus as the promised Messiah and teacher, written with Jewish readers in mind. It includes the Sermon on the Mount.

Mark.author: Traditionally John Mark, drawing on Peter's preaching
Mark.date: Around AD 65-70; probably the earliest Gospel
Mark.about: A fast-paced account of Jesus' actions, his suffering and his death.

Luke.author: Traditionally Luke, a physician and companion of Paul
Luke.about: An orderly account of Jesus' life, with special attention to the poor, women and outsiders. Written to someone named Theophilus.

John.author: Traditionally the apostle John
John.about: A reflective account built around Jesus' 'signs' and long speeches, including the 'I am' sayings.

Acts.author: The same author as Luke
Acts.about: The spread of the early church from Jerusalem to Rome, following Peter and then Paul.

Romans.author: Paul
Romans.about: Paul's fullest explanation of the gospel, and how Jewish and Gentile believers should live together, written to the church in Rome.

1 Corinthians.author: Paul
1 Corinthians.about: Advice to a divided church in Corinth about unity, ethics, worship, love (chapter 13) and the resurrection.

2 Corinthians.author: Paul
2 Corinthians.about: Paul defends his ministry and writes about strength in weakness, comfort in suffering and generous giving.

Galatians.author: Paul
Galatians.about: A passionate argument that Gentile Christians are free in Christ and don't need to adopt the Jewish law.

Ephesians.author: Traditionally Paul; some scholars think a follower wrote it
Ephesians.date: Around AD 60-62, or later if not by Paul
Ephesians.about: God's plan to unite all people in Christ, and what a new way of life looks like.

Philippians.author: Paul, writing from prison
Philippians.about: A warm letter about joy, humility and Christ's example, written to a church Paul loved.

Colossians.author: Traditionally Paul; debated by some scholars
Colossians.date: Around AD 60-62, or later if not by Paul
Colossians.about: Christ's supremacy over everything, and the new life that follows from it.

1 Thessalonians.author: Paul
1 Thessalonians.date: Around AD 50; possibly the earliest New Testament writing
1 Thessalonians.about: Encouragement to a young church, including hope about believers who have died.

2 Thessalonians.author: Traditionally Paul; debated by some scholars
2 Thessalonians.date: Around AD 51, or later if not by Paul
2 Thessalonians.about: Corrects confusion about the 'day of the Lord' and tells believers to keep working rather than sit idle.

1 Timothy.author: Traditionally Paul; many scholars think a later follower wrote it
1 Timothy.date: Debated: the 60s AD, or late 1st to early 2nd century
1 Timothy.about: Instructions to Timothy for leading the church at Ephesus.

2 Timothy.author: Traditionally Paul; many scholars think a later follower wrote it
2 Timothy.date: Debated: the mid-60s AD, or later
2 Timothy.about: A personal final charge to Timothy, written from prison.

Titus.author: Traditionally Paul; many scholars think a later follower wrote it
Titus.about: Instructions to Titus for organizing churches on Crete and encouraging good conduct.

Philemon.author: Paul
Philemon.about: A short personal letter asking Philemon to welcome back Onesimus, an enslaved man, 'no longer as a slave, but as a beloved brother.'

Hebrews.author: Unknown; Paul, Apollos and others have been suggested
Hebrews.about: Jesus as the greater high priest and the fulfillment of Israel's worship, with a call to endure.

James.author: Traditionally James, the brother of Jesus
James.date: Traditionally AD 45-62; some scholars date it later
James.about: Practical wisdom: faith shown through action, control of the tongue, and care for the poor.

1 Peter.author: Traditionally the apostle Peter
1 Peter.about: Encouragement to Christians scattered across Asia Minor who were suffering for their faith.

2 Peter.author: Traditionally the apostle Peter; many scholars think it is later
2 Peter.date: Debated: the 60s AD, or the early 2nd century
2 Peter.about: Warnings against false teachers and reassurance about Christ's return.

1 John.author: Traditionally the apostle John
1 John.about: God is love, so believers must love one another, and that love shows up in action.

2 John.author: Traditionally the apostle John ('the elder')
2 John.about: A very short letter urging a church to walk in love and truth.

3 John.author: Traditionally the apostle John ('the elder')
3 John.about: A very short personal letter about showing hospitality to traveling teachers.

Jude.author: Traditionally Jude, the brother of James
Jude.about: A brief, urgent warning against false teachers, encouraging readers to keep the faith.

Revelation.author: John, writing from the island of Patmos
Revelation.about: Vivid symbolic visions of the struggle between good and evil, ending with God making all things new.
